arXiv:2603.01960v1 [cs.LG] 02 Mar 2026

TiledAttention: a CUDA Tile SDPA Kernel for PyTorch

Taimur Khan Affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research - UFZ
Abstract

TiledAttention is a scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) forward operator for SDPA research on NVIDIA GPUs. Implemented in cuTile Python (TileIR) and exposed as a PyTorch-callable function, it is easier to modify than low-level CUDA templates while retaining realistic behavior via online softmax and tiled K,VK,V streaming. The approach is both performant and directly editable at the schedule level from Python (tile shapes, staging, shared-memory layout), enabling rapid, reproducible kernel research without template-heavy CUDA/CUTLASS rewrites. We benchmark TiledAttention on an NVIDIA DGX GB10 node with a reproducible harness and compare against PyTorch SDPA (auto-dispatch) and explicit unfused baselines across sequence length, head dimension, and precision (FP16/BF16). While production fused baselines remain stronger overall, TiledAttention delivers large speedups over standard eager attention paths and is available for direct use within PyTorch workflows, providing a practical balance between performance and customizability. Code: https://github.com/thisistaimur/TiledAttention Supplementary Material: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18787737

Keywords: 
attention SDPAHPC engineering tiling GPUs pytorch CUDA

1 Introduction

Foundation models in both language and vision increasingly rely on long-context attention, making scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) a recurring bottleneck in training and inference [7, 2, 3, 17, 8, 13]. In the long-sequence regime, attention becomes strongly bandwidth- and locality-sensitive, so kernel schedule quality directly affects throughput. This focus is also practical for European HPC deployments, where CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU systems remain common in recent EuroHPC and TOP500 snapshots [18, 16].

Tiling partitions the computation into blocks sized for on-chip memory and high data reuse; in attention this corresponds to blockwise score/softmax updates while streaming K,VK,V tiles. Recent CUDA Tile / TileIR and cuTile Python expose these schedule choices at a higher level than template-heavy CUDA development [12, 15, 4].

For SDPA research, a persistent issue is iteration cost: many high-performance kernels are difficult to modify without deep low-level changes, which slows experimentation with new attention variants. This paper studies TiledAttention, an online-softmax tiled SDPAforward operator expressed as a cuTile Python kernel. Our goal is to provide a simple and modifiable kernel for rapid, reproducible attention-kernel experimentation on DGX-class CUDA systems. The broader literature spans early neural attention, transformer-era SDPA, and efficient alternatives for long context [1, 19, 14, 9, 5].

Figure 1 gives a high-level intuition: as sequence length SS increases, SDPAincreasingly dominates end-to-end throughput.

Contributions. We make three contributions:

  • •

    Modifiable cuTile SDPAkernel: a forward SDPAoperator expressed as a Python tile program with online softmax updates and no materialization of the full attention matrix.

  • •

    DGX-ready reproducibility workflow: a measurement suite with explicit warmup, timing, correctness checks, and version pinning, demonstrated on DGX GB10 and portable to other DGX systems.

  • •

    FM-oriented evidence for text and vision regimes: scaling trends across sequence length SS, head dimension DD, and dtype (FP16/BF16), plus sensitivity analysis over key tiling parameters for foundation-model use cases [7, 2, 3, 17, 8, 13].

The rest of the paper follows the following organization: Section 2 presents the method, Section 3 gives implementation and evaluation details, and Section 4 reports results.

2 Method

2.1 Scaled dot-product attention

Given queries Q∈ℝS×DQ\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D}, keys K∈ℝS×DK\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D}, and values V∈ℝS×DV\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times D}, SDPAcomputes

O=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤D+M)​V,O=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{D}}+M\right)V, (1)

where MM is a mask (e.g., causal or padding). Materializing the score matrix Q​K⊤∈ℝS×SQK^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S} is prohibitive for long SS, motivating blockwise implementations.

2.2 Online softmax and blockwise attention

The FlashAttention line of work [5, 6] established blockwise, IO-aware attention as a strong baseline. It streams K,VK,V tiles while maintaining running softmax statistics (running max and normalization), avoiding materialization of the S×SS\times S score matrix.

2.3 Implementations and customization trade-offs

Production-grade attention kernels are often written in low-level CUDA/CUTLASS-style templates or JIT-compiled DSLs (e.g., Triton). While these achieve high performance, the implementation complexity can make it hard to (i) explore alternative schedules, (ii) isolate bottlenecks, and (iii) reproduce results across environments.

cuTile Python offers a tile-programming model that maps to a CUDA tile IR, keeping the kernel surface area accessible while enabling realistic schedules on modern GPUs. TiledAttention uses this model to expose tiling/staging parameters directly in Python.

Table 1 summarizes the high-level positioning of TiledAttention versus the fused SDPA baseline used in our evaluation.

3 Details

We target a systems-oriented kernel study with three explicit goals.

G1: Real and modifiable kernel in cuTile.

Implement SDPAforward with online softmax and masking, not a simplified microkernel, while keeping schedule choices easy to change.

G2: FM-relevant scaling for text and vision.

Track a strong baseline across shape regimes representative of deployed foundation models, especially D=64D{=}64/128128 and S∈[512,8192]S\in[512,8192] [7, 2, 3, 17, 8, 13].

G3: Transparent reproducibility.

Provide a benchmark harness and reporting that make results repeatable and interpretable across DGX-class CUDA systems.

We focus on the forward operator because it is (i) a common inference hot spot and (ii) an easier baseline to validate correctness and performance before extending to backward, KV-cache, and fused epilogues.

3.1 TiledAttention Kernel Design

Tensor shapes and layout

We assume inputs q,k,vq,k,v with shape [B,H,S,D][B,H,S,D]. For kernel execution, we reshape to [B​H,S,D][BH,S,D] and tile the SS dimension. To enable coalesced key loads, we access K⊤K^{\top} (conceptually Kt∈ℝB​H×D×SK_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{BH\times D\times S}).

Blockwise online softmax

Each cooperative thread array (CTA) owns a block of queries Qtile∈ℝTM×DQ_{\mathrm{tile}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{M}\times D} and streams tiles of K,VK,V along the sequence dimension. For each K,VK,V tile, the kernel computes partial scores Si​j=⟨qi,kj⟩/DS_{ij}=\langle q_{i},k_{j}\rangle/\sqrt{D}, applies a mask, and updates the online softmax state.

We maintain, per query row ii in the CTA tile:

mi\displaystyle m_{i} ←max⁡(mi,maxj⁡Si​j),\displaystyle\leftarrow\max(m_{i},\max_{j}S_{ij}), (2)
ℓi\displaystyle\ell_{i} ←ℓi⋅emiold−mi+∑jeSi​j−mi,\displaystyle\leftarrow\ell_{i}\cdot e^{m_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}-m_{i}}+\sum_{j}e^{S_{ij}-m_{i}}, (3)
oi\displaystyle o_{i} ←oi⋅emiold−mi+∑jeSi​j−mi​vj,\displaystyle\leftarrow o_{i}\cdot e^{m_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}-m_{i}}+\sum_{j}e^{S_{ij}-m_{i}}v_{j}, (4)

where mim_{i} is the running max, ℓi\ell_{i} is the running normalizer, and oi∈ℝDo_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is the running output accumulator. After streaming all tiles, we write Oi=oi/ℓiO_{i}=o_{i}/\ell_{i}.

Numerical choices

Inputs are FP16 or BF16. We accumulate dot products, softmax statistics, and output accumulation in FP32 for stability (matching common practice in high-performance attention kernels). We optionally support causal and padding masks; causal masking avoids reading or contributing to tiles strictly above the diagonal.

3.2 Implementation

API

We expose a minimal functional API:

sdpa(q, k, v, causal, scale)→o.\texttt{sdpa(q, k, v, causal, scale)}\rightarrow\texttt{o}. (5)

The API matches common frameworks: q,k,v are contiguous tensors in [B,H,S,D][B,H,S,D], causal selects causal masking, and scale defaults to 1/D1/\sqrt{D}.

PyTorch entry point.

TiledAttention is available as a Python package that integrates with PyTorch. A typical usage pattern is:

import torch
from tiledattention import sdpa

# q,k,v must be CUDA tensors with dtype float16 or bfloat16.
o = sdpa(q, k, v, causal=True)  # q,k,v: [B, H, S, D]

Compilation and caching

The cuTile kernel is JIT-compiled and cached by a key (TM,TN,D,dtype,causal)(T_{M},T_{N},D,\mathrm{dtype},\mathrm{causal}), avoiding recompilation and ensuring steady-state measurement.

Benchmark harness

We evaluate kernels using a reproducible harness with the following policies:

  • •

    Warmup: run NwN_{w} iterations to trigger compilation and stabilize clocks.

  • •

    Timing: CUDA events around the forward call; report median and p95 over NrN_{r} repetitions.

  • •

    Correctness: for small shapes (e.g., S≤256S\leq 256), compare to a high-precision reference (FP32) within a tolerance that accounts for FP16/BF16.

  • •

    Isolation: synchronize before timing, avoid interleaving other GPU work.

All runs are executed on a DGX GB10 node; the same scripts apply to other DGX systems with CUDA-compatible stacks.

3.3 Experimental Setup

We sweep a workload grid intended to cover common foundation-model attention shapes:

  • •

    Sequence length S∈{512,1024,2048,4096,8192}S\in\{512,1024,2048,4096,8192\}.

  • •

    Head dimensions D∈{64,96,128,160}D\in\{64,96,128,160\}.

  • •

    Dtypes: FP16 and BF16.

  • •

    Masking: causal and non-causal.

This grid is anchored in common transformer deployments: D=64D{=}64 is common in BERT- and ViT-style models [7, 8, 13], while D=128D{=}128 is prevalent in larger decoder-only language models such as GPT-3, PaLM, and LLaMA-family systems [2, 3, 17]. Sequence lengths 512–2048 cover short-to-mid context workloads common in serving and fine-tuning, while 4096–8192 capture long-context pressure in modern FM deployments.

We compare TiledAttention to fused PyTorch SDPA on the same node with identical tensor initialization, streams, and timing methodology. We also report explicit unfused baselines (torch_sdpa_math and standard eager attention) for context.

4 Results

The full results of the benchmark with summaries and NSight [11] logs are available in the Supplementary Material [10]. We report (i) time per forward and (ii) throughput, normalized to tokens/s for interpretability (BB: batch, HH: heads, SS: sequence).

Throughput=B⋅H⋅Stime(tokens/s).\mathrm{Throughput}=\frac{B\cdot H\cdot S}{\mathrm{time}}\quad\text{(tokens/s)}. (6)

4.1 Throughput scaling vs sequence length

Figure 3 plots throughput versus SS for FP16 and BF16; long-SS trends reflect memory traffic, while short-SS is overhead- and utilization-limited.

Observed behavior in our runs.

Across the full study grid (80 points: S∈{512,1024,2048,4096,8192}S\in\{512,1024,2048,4096,8192\}, D∈{64,96,128,160}D\in\{64,96,128,160\}, FP16/BF16, causal/non-causal), TiledAttention achieves a mean throughput ratio of 0.632×0.632\times versus fused PyTorch SDPA (median 0.634×0.634\times), with 4 wins out of 80 points. The closest regime is D=128D{=}128 (mean 0.947×0.947\times, 4/20 wins). For D∈{64,96,160}D\in\{64,96,160\}, fused SDPA remains faster on average. We also observe a transition around S≈2048S\approx 2048: short-SS points can approach parity, while long-SS becomes more sensitive to memory traffic and instruction mix. For example, in FP16 non-causal at D=128D{=}128, TiledAttention reaches 73.6273.62 TFLOP/s at S=4096S{=}4096 versus 78.9878.98 for fused SDPA, and 73.3873.38 versus 88.8488.84 at S=8192S{=}8192.

4.2 Explicit baseline summary

To make the value proposition explicit for HPC users, we report TiledAttention not only against fused PyTorch SDPA, but also against unfused baselines. Table 4 shows that while fused SDPA is still the strongest overall baseline, TiledAttention provides large speedups over standard eager attention and PyTorch’s math SDPA path across the full grid.

4.3 Regime map over (S,D)(S,D)

A regime heatmap is a compact way to summarize which shapes are competitive. Figure 5 illustrates the intended presentation: cells show TiledAttention performance as a percentage of fused PyTorch SDPA (100% is parity).

In the measured regime map, the largest gaps appear at higher or non-power-of-two head dimensions (notably D=160D{=}160 and D=96D{=}96), while D=128D{=}128 remains closest to parity. Averaged over all sequence lengths, dtypes, and masking modes, throughput ratios (TiledAttention/fused SDPA) are: D=64:0.727×D{=}64:0.727\times, D=96:0.513×D{=}96:0.513\times, D=128:0.947×D{=}128:0.947\times, D=160:0.343×D{=}160:0.343\times.

4.4 Profiling-guided bottleneck analysis

To interpret scaling trends, we profile representative shapes with Nsight Compute (counters) and Nsight Systems (timeline/API overhead). We track throughput, memory traffic, and stalls to identify when the kernel becomes memory-bound, what limits short-SS, and which knobs move these regimes.

In our experience, long-SS shapes show high shared- and global-memory pressure, so staging depth and shared-memory layout can dominate. Short-SS shapes can be limited by insufficient parallelism and overheads, where larger TMT_{M} may help at the cost of occupancy.

For non-causal FP16 at B=1,H=8,S=4096,D=128B{=}1,H{=}8,S{=}4096,D{=}128, one-pass Nsight Compute shows TiledAttention at 1.1761.176 ms versus fused SDPA at 1.1031.103 ms for the primary kernel. At S=2048,D=64S{=}2048,D{=}64, the kernels are near parity (TiledAttention 0.21030.2103 ms, fused SDPA 0.20950.2095 ms). For causal S=4096,D=128S{=}4096,D{=}128, TiledAttention reports 0.66960.6696 ms versus 0.63020.6302 ms for fused SDPA. Overall, this confirms the same shape-dependent profile: the gap is narrowest in the tuned D=64D{=}64 regime and wider at longer D=128D{=}128 sequences. For reproducibility, we provide raw profiler artifacts and summaries in the supplemtary matrials: ncu_*.ncu-rep, ncu_*_raw.csv, and ncu_profile_summary_*.md; timeline traces are included as *.nsys-rep when collected.

4.5 Sensitivity to tiling parameters

A central advantage of expressing the kernel as a tile program is the ability to expose and sweep tiling parameters. Table 5 summarizes the best-performing tile settings by regime and reports sensitivity: how far performance drops when using a non-optimal but reasonable tile choice.

4.6 Optimization ladder on reduced benchmark

To show what the tile-programming workflow provides in practice, Table 6 reports a focused reduced benchmark before/after schedule-policy refinements. The key point is not a universal win from one static configuration, but that a shape-aware policy recovers performance across mixed regimes without low-level CUDA rewrites.

5 Discussion

Across our runs, two knobs dominate first-order behavior: tile sizes (TM,TN)(T_{M},T_{N}) and staging depth. Larger tiles can improve reuse and streaming efficiency but may reduce occupancy through shared-memory and register pressure. Reliable comparison therefore requires a stable harness (warmup, isolated stream, median/p95 reporting), especially with JIT-compiled kernels.

When should HPC users adopt TiledAttention?

Table 7 summarizes a pragmatic deployment view. The primary advantage is controllability and iteration speed for architecture-specific tuning and research, while fused SDPA remains the default for maximum out-of-the-box throughput.

Strong competitors make custom-kernel value clearer.

The FlashAttention family [5, 6] remains a strong external competitor and sets a high bar for attention performance. Against that context, the value of TiledAttention is practical: fast kernel iteration, clear schedule controls, and reproducible profiling for architecture-specific tuning in HPC settings.

Why short-SS can win while long-SS loses.

At short sequence lengths, tuned tile shapes can deliver good locality and low overhead, yielding isolated wins (e.g., S=512,D=128S{=}512,D{=}128). Around S≈2048S\approx 2048, the kernel transitions from an overhead-sensitive regime to a sustained streaming regime. As SS increases further, the number of streamed tiles and online-softmax update work grows, and the current kernel’s occupancy/instruction-mix limitations become more visible. In contrast, fused production SDPA kernels maintain higher sustained throughput in the long-context regime.

6 Limitations and Future Work

This work has three main limitations. First, we evaluate only the forward pass; backward and fused variants are future work. Second, we target Grace–Blackwell / Blackwell-class GPUs; portability to other architectures may require additional schedules. Third, we study a deliberately small tuning space; extending to larger search spaces is an important next step.

7 Conclusion

We presented TiledAttention, a tiled online-softmax SDPAforward operator expressed as a cuTile Python tile program on Grace–Blackwell. Beyond a kernel implementation, we contributed a reproducible benchmark harness and an analysis that highlights how performance scales with sequence length, head dimension, dtype, and tiling choices. Our results support a practical workflow for performance engineering of foundation-model primitives on HPC systems.
